Islam therefore found a mature language and a mature system of expression already available to it.

That language was capable not only of expressing the historical conditions that had made the rise of Islam possible. It was also capable of expressing the new historical possibilities that opened after Islam appeared.

The language of the Qur'an, which reaches the highest levels of Arabic expression, is therefore one of the most important signs of historical continuity in the development of Arab society before Islam, even as that continuity also contained dialectical breaks.
This mature language was not simply a linguistic phenomenon. At its core, it was a social phenomenon.
The advanced form in which Arabic appears in the Qur'an was one expression of the culture that had developed during the pre-Islamic period.
Could such a language, together with the artistic power it displays in both poetry and prose, really have been produced in only a century and a half before Islam?
Scientific reasoning completely rejects such an ahistorical idea.

One Western thinker expresses surprise at how quickly Arabic became a shared language of scholarship among the different peoples who belonged to Islamic civilization. He also notes how Arabic “shaped, through its own structure, some of the most significant features of Islamic thought; even Greek concepts underwent deep changes as they passed through this structure.”
A historical materialist view of this important development assumes that a long history lay behind it—a history stretching back several centuries before the period immediately preceding Islam.
Repeated breaks in that long history may have caused later generations to lose knowledge of important stages in the development of Arabic and of pre-Islamic poetry before the fifth century CE.
But that does not change the objective reality itself.
Not knowing that something existed does not mean that it did not exist.
Later, we will return to the historical development of pre-Islamic poetry and other cultural features.
Here we are concerned with geography, geology, and climate, and with the effect these conditions had on the ancient distribution of the population across the Arabian Peninsula.
We do not mean that these natural conditions directly determined the economic and social relationships that appeared during different stages of Arab history before Islam.

At the same time, however, we should not ignore the part they played in shaping the early division of labor in some parts of the peninsula and in influencing the first directions taken by pre-Islamic society.

When we look at the geography of the Arabian Peninsula, one issue immediately stands out. Early Arab geographers disagreed about where its northern boundaries had lain before Islam, as we can see from Yaqut.

Al-Hamdani, who wrote in the fourth Islamic century and therefore lived before Yaqut, places the lower Euphrates at the peninsula’s northeastern boundary and the Mediterranean coast of Palestine at its northwestern boundary.

Belyaev, writing in modern times, doubts that al-Hamdani’s exact boundaries were correct. But he does not doubt that the Syrian Desert was considered part of Arabia before Islam. He also argues that in the fifth and sixth centuries, the political boundary between the Persian and Byzantine empires left the Syrian Desert in the hands of its native population: the Arabs.
Ibn Hawqal gives us evidence supporting the same view, and we may find further support in Ibn Khaldun. He writes:

“... Between the Persian Sea and the Qulzum lies the Arabian Peninsula, as though it were a piece of land projecting into the sea. It is surrounded by the Abyssinian Sea to the south, the Sea of Qulzum to the west, and the Persian Sea to the east, extending toward Iraq between Syria and Basra, with a distance of fifteen hundred miles between them.”

There is, of course, no real disagreement over the peninsula’s other boundaries. They are naturally marked by three seas: the Indian Ocean or Arabian Sea to the south, the Arabian-Persian Gulf to the east, and the Red Sea—known in earlier times as the Sea of Qulzum—to the west.
Ancient Greek and Roman geographers divided the Arabian Peninsula differently from Arab geographers of the medieval period.
The Greeks and Romans, working from the political situation of Arabia in the first century CE, divided it into three parts:
a. The desert region in the north, southwest of the Syrian Desert, where the Nabataean kingdom was located.
c. The desert region where nomadic tribes were dominant.
Arab geographers, by contrast, seem to have based their divisions mainly on natural geography and geology, and perhaps partly on economic conditions as well.
They divided the peninsula into five regions: Tihama, the Hijaz, Najd, al-Arud, and Yemen.
This division appears in al-Hamdani and Yaqut. Ibn Hawqal seems to have followed it too, judging from Ibn al-Faqih’s account of the boundaries assigned to each of these five regions.
Ibn Hawqal also adds the Iraqi Desert, the Jazira Desert between the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Syrian Desert.
The climate of the Arabian Peninsula follows from its geography and differs from one region to another.
Because most of the peninsula is desert, dryness is the dominant condition. Rainfall is irregular, and rainwater generally does not collect into regular, permanent waterways.

There are, however, regions with fertile soil and milder climates. These include Yemen and Hadramawt in the south, the mountains around Taif near Mecca, the city of Yathrib—later Medina—in the north, and Yamama in the southeast.
These differences shaped both the way people lived and the early division of labor.
In dry regions, unsettled nomadic life became dominant. People depended on livestock and moved in search of seasonal pasture and temporary sources of water.

In regions suited to agriculture, settled and more urban forms of life appeared. People farmed as well as raising livestock, and small craft industries developed to meet the needs of settled agricultural communities.
Other areas, especially the oases, produced a way of life that was partly settled and partly nomadic.

People there stayed in the oases during parts of the year to grow dates, some grains, and vegetables, especially toward the end of winter. During the rest of the year they moved with their animals, mainly camels, in search of pasture.
When they left, they would often leave some members of their families behind to protect the crops until they returned for the harvest.
The life of these oasis communities was part of a very long historical process through which nomadic groups gradually became settled communities tied to work on the land.
Looking at the picture in broad terms, we can divide the population of the Arabian Peninsula in the final pre-Islamic period into three groups according to how they produced the means of life.
The first was settled and worked mainly in agriculture.
The second was unsettled and depended on herding and migration.
The third lived between settlement and migration and represented a transitional stage from the second, lower condition to the first, higher one.
Each of these groups therefore represented a different early stage in the long human struggle to gain greater control over nature and produce the means of life.
From the earliest stages of this struggle, human beings advanced by developing the relationship between physical labor and intellectual labor.
The differences between these three groups still reflected a stage at which the production of basic necessities depended heavily on natural conditions, especially geography and climate.
This dependence marked human labor before people became able to free themselves from the absolute control of such conditions.
The people of the Arabian Peninsula did not, however, remain completely trapped by this dependence on nature.

Toward the end of the final pre-Islamic period, we begin to see ways in which they slowly and partially learned to make use of the possibilities offered by their geographical position, climate, and natural resources.
We can see this in several developments:
They took advantage of the Arabian Peninsula’s location on major trade routes connecting different parts of the inhabited world.
This position created income from services provided along caravan routes and led to growing trade, through which the use of money began to spread.
These conditions allowed productive activity to grow and private ownership of the means of production to appear in forms specific to that historical stage.

Where water and suitable soil were available, people used them for artificial irrigation and for growing a wider range of crops, including fruit, grain, and legumes. In this way they increased the productivity of the land.

Small craft industries producing everyday goods also appeared. People worked with metals, clay, and leather to make weapons, iron farming tools, pottery, and tanned leather. These crafts began to separate from agriculture.
These material developments were the main forces shaping the direction in which pre-Islamic tribal society changed.
This does not mean that society became completely independent of natural conditions. Such independence is neither assumed nor possible, because human society does not exist outside nature.
What is possible—and historically necessary—is for human beings to gain increasing control over these natural conditions and make the fullest possible use of them.

This growing human control gives the development of each society its particular historical character, while the general laws governing the development of human societies continue to operate across all of them, however different their local conditions may be.
3 — The Direction of Change in the Economic Structure

We can trace this direction by following the historical development of the same features discussed above. As we do so, one thing becomes especially clear: by the end of the sixth century CE, these different parts of the economy were interacting with one another in a noticeable way.

The clearest example was the growing connection between agriculture and trade. Each helped the other develop. The use of iron tools in farming—including iron ploughs—together with artificial irrigation increased the production of grain and vegetables. This created a relative surplus beyond immediate local needs. At the same time, that surplus made it possible for trade to expand. Agricultural produce now became part of commercial exchange. In other words, it was increasingly being produced for exchange rather than simply for local consumption. It was becoming commodity production.
We can therefore see agriculture and trade influencing each other. To make this picture clearer, we need to look at some of the historical evidence.

Trade: Accounts of periods before the Jāhiliyya tell us about the flourishing trade route once known in Arabia as the “Perfume Route” or “Incense Route.” Perfumes, incense, and similar goods travelled along it between India, Yemen, and the Mediterranean lands.

This route had already flourished under the Minaeans and Sabaeans during the first millennium BCE. The two peoples competed for control over it, including the oases through which it passed in the north-west of the peninsula.

Later, however, the route lost its commercial importance. After the Minaeans, the Sabaeans also lost control of the Red Sea and the coast of East Africa as maritime trade passed into Greek and Roman hands. During the first Himyarite state, in 24 BCE, the Romans even tried to seize Yemen itself so that they could control the region’s overland trade routes as well.

That attempt failed, but Roman control of the Red Sea was enough to destroy the commercial importance of the Perfume Route. It badly damaged both the trading and agricultural economy of Yemen, adding to the damage caused by the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam at around the same time.

Following Jawād ʿAlī, we can even say that the collapse of the dam itself may have been one result of Roman control of Red Sea trade. The Himyarites lost so much of their commercial wealth that they no longer had the resources to maintain and repair the dam properly. Eventually, it collapsed.

The Perfume Route later recovered its importance. This happened after the Byzantine Empire formed an alliance with Abyssinia and helped the Abyssinians conquer Yemen. Abyssinian influence then spread over the Red Sea trade routes and the old overland route running from the south of the peninsula to the north. This helped secure Byzantine trade with India.

From the second third of the sixth century CE onward, the Perfume Route once again became an important part of international trade. Goods travelled along it between India, Yemen, Palestine, Egypt, Greece, and other parts of the Byzantine Empire.
Alongside it ran another route carrying goods that had crossed the Red Sea from East Africa—especially Somalia and Eritrea—through al-Yamāma and on to Iraq.

Arabia had therefore become a meeting point for some of the most important trade routes connecting the populated worlds of East and West. This was true of the south and north of the peninsula, as well as its east and west. Both major routes connected south with north: one from the eastern side, the other from the western side.

The Ḥijāz in particular occupied an unusually important position. It lay between trade routes coming from the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea across the Arabian Peninsula, and routes coming from Persia, Iraq, Syria, and the wider Mediterranean world. It stood, in effect, at the centre of a network connecting the two great empires of that age: the Sasanian Persian Empire and the Byzantine Empire.

This location played a major part in the growth of trading towns in the Ḥijāz. These towns became commercial stations along the Red Sea route. Trading ports also developed where Roman ships could take on goods and products from India. Among them were al-Shuʿayba, the old port of Mecca before Jeddah became its main port, and Yanbuʿ, the port of Yathrib.

The commercial importance of the Ḥijāz grew further after Abyssinian rule in Yemen came to an end and was replaced by Persian rule. Byzantine influence then withdrew from southern Arabia and from the Red Sea route. The two overland routes to India regained their earlier importance: one through the Euphrates and Tigris region, and the other through Yemen and Syria by way of Mecca. As a result, “al-Ḥīra under the Lakhmids and Mecca under Banū al-Naḍr made enormous gains.”

By the end of the sixth century CE, the gains made by Mecca were increasingly concentrated in the hands of Quraysh’s leading families. Other tribal chiefs also profited when important trade routes passed through their territories.
The leaders of Quraysh themselves had by then become the main middlemen in international trade between India and China on one side, and the Mediterranean lands and East Africa on the other.

Their commercial and financial power became so great, on top of their traditional tribal authority, that they imposed dues and taxes on smaller Arab merchants who were not allied with them, as well as on foreign merchants.
Foreign traders also had a noticeable presence in Mecca, according to the Arabic sources. They included Romans and Persians who had commercial ties with the great Qurayshi merchants.
We should also remember that Mecca’s religious position as the home of the Kaʿba gave the leaders of Quraysh another source of wealth and helped strengthen the city’s commercial importance.
Agriculture: It is generally accepted that during the two centuries before the rise of Islam, Bedouins made up a larger share of Arabia’s population than settled people tied to the land.

But this is only a broad impression. The historical sources from the period give us no statistical figures, even approximate ones. We therefore cannot use this general fact as a firm basis for a strict analysis of the social and economic structure of pre-Islamic society.
The usual impression is that Bedouins greatly outnumbered settled people. Many analyses of the economic and social structure have therefore been built on this vague overall assumption.

Yet we also have a great deal of historical evidence pointing in another direction. Many places across the peninsula had people who irrigated and cultivated the land and who had considerable farming knowledge. In many areas, production sometimes exceeded local consumption needs and the surplus entered local markets for exchange.

This was not limited to one part of Arabia. Agriculture was certainly more widespread in some regions, especially the south, than in others. Yemen, for example, had lost some of the relative agricultural prosperity it had enjoyed when the Maʾrib Dam was still intact.
